papers.title: CAREERPILOT AI
papers.abstract: The increasing competition in the employment market has created significant challenges for students and job seekers in preparing effective resumes, identifying relevant skills, and performing effectively in interviews. Existing career-support systems commonly address individual tasks such as resume screening, job recommendation, or interview preparation, while providing limited integration and personalization. This paper proposes CareerPilot AI, an intelligent career assistance system that integrates resume analysis, Applicant Tracking System evaluation, job-description matching, skill-gap identification, AI-based mock interviews, response evaluation, and personalized learning-roadmap generation. The proposed system uses Natural Language Processing, Large Language Models, semantic matching, and Retrieval-Augmented Generation to process user information and generate context-aware recommendations. A web-based architecture using Streamlit and FastAPI or Flask is proposed, with PDF parsing libraries for resume extraction and vector databases for retrieval-based services. The evaluation framework measures resume parsing accuracy, resume-job matching performance, skill-gap identification, interview-response evaluation, response time, and usability. The system is designed to provide an integrated digital career mentor that connects a candidate's current profile with target job requirements and subsequent preparation activities. Actual experimental results will be obtained after implementation and testing.

papers.title: An Explainable Multi-Agent System for Real-Time SMS Smishing Detection with LangGraph Orchestration
papers.abstract: SMS has become a target for cyberattacks. Users may get one-time passwords, transaction notifications, banking alerts and other service announcements.These messages can be quite familiar, urgent, making it difficult to determine fake messages, putting users at risk of being victims of smishing. Once successful, information and authentication credentials can be stolen from victims.Current defenses are typically designed with static rules or individual AI models. They struggle to catch evolving scam messages. They also lack real-time analysis, a combined threat check and clear reasons for why a message's dangerous. To solve these problems we introduce ScamShield AI. ScamShield AI is a multi-agent AI system that works in time to detect smishing. It contains three agents: an OTP Message Analysis Agent, a Contact Trust and Pattern Recognition Agent and a URL Analysis Agent. Each agent looks at a part of an incoming SMS. A LangGraph-based Coordinator Agent brings the agents together combines their results and outputs a label of Safe, Suspicious or Scam along with a risk score. The system first cleans messages and creates semantic embeddings for similarity-based threat detection. A MongoDB community database uses vector search to find messages that're semantically similar to known scam patterns. If the message matches known harmful patterns, the system doesn't have to analyze it. New messages go through the LangGraph multi-agent pipeline. Security controls keep the threat data trustworthy. In addition the system uses Explainable AI to give users an explanation of why a message is determined to be suspicious. the app can suggest steps that users can take, for instance, refraining from clicking on links or blocking the sender, which can help them make better security decisions.

papers.title: Agentic AI-Based Indian Legal Notice and Complaint Understanding with Source-Grounded Next-Step Guidance
papers.abstract: This paper proposes an Agentic AI-based architecture for understanding Indian legal notices and complaints using Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) and Explainable AI (XAI). The proposed system aims to help ordinary citizens understand complex legal documents by extracting key information, identifying relevant legal provisions, and providing source-grounded explanations and next-step guidance. The architecture consists of an Orchestrator Agent and six specialized agents: Document Analysis, Legal Research, Summarization, Explainability, Next-Step Guidance, and Validation. It combines BM25 keyword search with FAISS dense-vector retrieval and cross-encoder re-ranking to identify relevant Indian statutes and legal references. The proposed generation component uses a LoRA-adapted LLaMA-3.1-8B-Instruct model. The system emphasizes traceability, factual grounding, and validation to reduce unsupported legal claims. It is intended to assist users in understanding legal documents and does not replace professional legal advice. This paper presents the proposed architecture and methodology, along with illustrative hypothetical case studies. Implementation and empirical evaluation remain future work.

papers.title: A Managed Database-as-a-Service Platform for Scientific Computing
papers.abstract: Scientific computing at HPC facilities increasingly relies on database infrastructure across a growing range of workloads: vector search and retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), structured analytics, and AI-driven knowledge discovery over community corpora spanning documentation, experimental datasets, simulation outputs, and literature collections. These corpora are inherently shared facility resources, serving researchers, facility support staff, and AI agents across projects and institutions. Yet the supporting infrastructure remains built per project: each team provisions, configures, and operates its own database instance, with no facility-level registry, no shared identity layer, and no uniform interface for discovering or accessing the databases hosted across the facility. Commercial cloud platforms have addressed analogous needs through managed Database-as-a-Service offerings (e.g., Amazon RDS, Snowflake, Pinecone). However, these solutions do not transfer cleanly to scientific computing: they rely on proprietary identity systems, cannot directly access facility filesystems, and incur substantial data egress costs. We are building the missing piece: a managed database platform that lives inside the HPC facility, developed and evaluated on ALCF Polaris. One federated sign-in (Globus) brings a researcher — or an AI agent acting on their behalf — to every database the facility hosts, through a web UI, a scriptable API, or the Model Context Protocol. Governance, catalog, and access control are handled once by the platform and inherited by every project by default. The central design choice is scaling, native to HPC. Each workload is decomposed into its resource-consuming stages, and each stage can be scaled independently across nodes. As one representative example, a vector-search workload scales GPU-based embedding generation and search-index serving independently across nodes, reaching 5,197 queries/sec on 8 nodes (4.3× single-node) on ALCF Polaris and still climbing at maximum tested concurrency. Governance adds modest overhead at single-user load and becomes negligible under concurrency. In an end-to-end RAG pipeline built on this workload, retrieval contributes under 2% of total latency — the bottleneck has moved entirely to LLM generation. The same decomposition pattern is designed to extend to other workload types as additional engine adapters are integrated. The talk presents what changes when scientific data services are native to the facility: who can use them, what AI agents become capable of, and how a single platform can replace per-project infrastructure across an entire lab. We will share the design tradeoffs, what the scaling numbers mean for facility capacity planning, and the next stage of the design — co-locating the database service with model-inference services and scaling both on demand against shared facility resources, planned for the coming year. We invite peer facilities to adopt the platform and collaborate with us on a unified, cross-facility scientific data service.

papers.title: Lossless Compression of Proximity Graph Indexes for Efficient Approximate Nearest Neighbors Search
papers.abstract: Graph-based Approximate Nearest Neighbor (ANN) indexes, such as HNSW, are the backbone of modern vector search. However, their massive memory footprint creates a severe infrastructure bottleneck. While vector quantization is widely adopted to reduce the memory required to store data vectors, the graph's edge structure increasingly dominates total memory usage. Compressing these adjacency lists for online search presents a critical system challenge: because decompression occurs during query processing, i.e., while navigating the graph, memory savings cannot come at the expense of query latency. In this paper, we present a compression technique explicitly tailored for live HNSW routing. By applying offline graph permutations to artificially induce structural locality, we enable the use of SIMD-accelerated integer compressors, such as Stream VByte, for rapid on-the-fly decompression. Evaluated across diverse real-world workloads, we significantly outperform the current state of the art in both compression ratio and query latency. Our experimental results show that we achieve compression ratios up to 52.7% with negligible penalties in latency compared to the uncompressed baseline. Furthermore, our technique has been effectively deployed in production at eBay, achieving up to 44.3% reduction in edge storage with no degradation in query latency.

papers.title: On Worst-Case Guarantees for Graph-Based Nearest-Neighbor Search
papers.abstract: Graph-based nearest neighbor search algorithms like HNSW, DiskANN, NSG, and others have surged in popularity in recent years due to their excellent empirical performance in comparison to space-partitioning methods like IVF data structures and Locality Sensitive Hashing (LSH). However, in contrast to LSH and related methods, obtaining strong worst-case theoretical guarantees for graph-based search has proven challenging. In this paper, we prove a strong lower bound that helps explain the lack of progress towards such guarantees. We show that no standard graph-based method (any that runs a variant of greedy search on a flat or hierarchical graph) can achieve sublinear query time for approximate nearest neighbor search in Euclidean space, even for an arbitrarily large approximation factor. On the other hand, we prove that sublinear query time is possible if we allow for Steiner points in the search graph. We obtain bounds comparable to LSH, showing e.g., that graph-based search with Steiner points can solve $c$-approximate nearest neighbor search in Euclidean space with query time $\tilde{O}(n^{1/(c-1)})$. We complement this result with initial experiments exploring how Steiner points can be incorporated into practical graph-based methods.

papers.title: Fast Sparse $α$-Navigable Graph Construction with Improved Resource Augmentation
papers.abstract: Graph-based nearest neighbor search methods, which run greedy search on a directed graph over the data points, have surged in popularity in recent years. A common goal is to construct a search graph with the $α$-navigability property, which ensures that greedy search returns provably good approximate nearest neighbors and converges in few iterations. Increasing $α\geq 1$ improves accuracy and convergence rate, but requires more edges, which increases both space and search time. This tradeoff has motivated the study of algorithms for constructing a sparsest $α$-navigable graph for a given set of points. For any point set and any distance function, we show how to compute an $α$-navigable graph with at most $O(\log n)$ times as many edges as the sparsest $(1+\varepsilon)α$-navigable graph, in $O(n^ω\log(Δ)/\varepsilon)$ time, where $ω< 2.372$ is the matrix multiplication exponent and $Δ$ is the aspect ratio of the input. This improves on Khanna, Padaki, and Waingarten (SODA 2026), who achieve the same runtime but are only competitive with the sparsest $2(1+\varepsilon)α$-navigable graph. Since sparsity often increases rapidly with $α$ (typically $α\leq 1.1$), their bound can be significantly weaker. Previously, the best algorithm competing with the sparsest $(1+\varepsilon)α$-navigable graph required $\widetilde{O}(n^{2.5})$ time. Our techniques also extend to constructing sparse $τ$-monotonic graphs, another popular target in nearest neighbor search. Finally, we give a fine-grained complexity analysis suggesting that improving the $O(n^ω)$ running time is unlikely, or would require a very different approach. It is based on hardness results for problems related to verifying whether a graph is navigable, a topic of independent interest.

papers.title: Fast Approximate Line Nearest Neighbor Search
papers.abstract: Approximate nearest neighbor (ANN) search, which retrieves vectors close to a given query vector, is a fundamental operation in vector databases. However, emerging applications, such as selecting source images for photo-based animation and video synthesis, may require matching content while allowing a query-specified aspect contrast, such as an illumination change, to vary; a single query point does not directly express this requirement. In this paper, we study approximate line nearest neighbor (LANN) search, where an infinite query line removes the distance contribution along a specified direction while database records remain points. Prior approaches focus on top-$1$ search only for LANN and can incur high construction costs. Converting LANN into ordinary point ANN search through dimension lifting substantially increases index construction and query costs, while direct search on a proximity graph built for ordinary point ANN search can miss distinct regions close to a line. To address these issues, we propose LinePG, which enhances an existing proximity graph with pair edges to facilitate navigation between separated near-line regions. To find these pair edges efficiently, we first generate region pairs with spatial or graph separation, and near a line. We then score edges between the selected region pairs to guide the point endpoint selections. We conduct extensive performance studies and confirm the accuracy and efficiency of LinePG in comparison with the baseline approaches.

papers.title: RAG-Based MCA AI Agent for Document-Grounded College Information Assistance Using Retrieval-Augmented Generation, Vector Search and a Locally Hosted Large Language Model
papers.abstract: This paper presents the design and implementation of a Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG)-based MCA AI Agent for document-grounded question answering over college and student policy documents. The system uses PyMuPDF for PDF text extraction, approximately 1000-character chunks, Nomic-Embed-Text for generating 768-dimensional embeddings, and Pinecone for semantic vector search. At query time, the system retrieves the three most relevant document chunks and provides them as context to Llama 3.2 running locally through Ollama. A React.js frontend and FastAPI backend provide the conversational interface. The paper describes the system architecture, methodology, implementation, document-refresh workflow, and practical deployment considerations, including stale vectors and local inference latency. It also outlines an evaluation framework for comparing a standalone LLM with the proposed RAG pipeline using retrieval relevance, answer correctness, faithfulness, and latency. The current work is presented as a system implementation and preliminary study. A controlled quantitative evaluation has not yet been completed, and no numerical accuracy improvement is claimed. Keywords: Retrieval-Augmented Generation, Large Language Models, Semantic Search, Vector Database, Pinecone, Llama 3.2, Ollama, FastAPI, React.js, Document-Grounded Question Answering.

papers.title: VecForge: A Local-First Hybrid Vector Database with Persistent Agent Memory and Order-Preserving Grover-Inspired Reranking
papers.abstract: Retrieval-augmented applications and AI assistants need a vector store that runs inside the user's own process, keeps data encrypted on disk, combines semantic and keyword retrieval, and remembers information across conversations. This paper presents VecForge 2.0, an embedded Python vector database built for these needs. One SQLite file, optionally encrypted with SQLCipher, holds documents, vectors, metadata, access keys, agent sessions and index snapshots. Queries fuse FAISS dense search with an incremental BM25 index, and namespace and deletion constraints apply inside both indexes. A memory layer, served over the Model Context Protocol, ranks memories by relevance, importance and recency. The paper also proves that the Grover-inspired reranker of the previous release applies only the diffusion half of Grover's algorithm, so it can only keep or reverse a ranking, and replaces it with an O(N) closed form of the full algorithm that preserves order. Eighteen experiments evaluate every feature. On the SciFact benchmark, hybrid fusion reaches an nDCG@10 of 0.707, against 0.645 for dense search, 0.665 for BM25 and 0.681 for reciprocal rank fusion. Compared with the previous release, in-index constraints raise recall in small namespaces from 0.5% to 100%, incremental indexing makes insertion 183 times faster, and snapshots make reopening 9 to 17 times faster, while encryption and access control add little cost. The evaluation also reports where the design falls short, including slow, highly selective filters and memory deduplication that confuses paraphrases with changed facts. A single local file can therefore serve both retrieval and long-term memory for AI agents.

papers.title: Retrieval Is the New Record System: A Retrospective Analysis of Open-Source Contributions to Vector Databases and Embedding Infrastructure Underpinning Clinical AI (2025-2026)
papers.abstract: Background. Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) sits inside many clinical artificial intelligence (AI) prototypes. A language model answers from documents a retrieval layer selects first. If that layer returns the wrong documents, or returns nothing and reports success, the error starts before the model generates a word. Vector databases and embedding tools form that retrieval layer in most designs, so their defects count as health infrastructure defects. Purpose. This study analysed one contributor's public pull request (PR) record in vector database and retrieval projects. It asked three practical questions in sequence. What kinds of defects did the contributions address? What share of the work reached merge? Where did the process break down? Methods. On 21 October 2026 I extracted my full PR record through the GitHub API (author:rtmalikian): 213 PRs across 94 repositories (85 external projects and 9 of the author's own repositories). I defined a subset for vector databases and retrieval infrastructure: 39 PRs across 8 repositories. I coded each PR by status at extraction and read the review threads of seven cases in depth. Two cases from projects next to the subset, cocoindex-io/cocoindex and sentence-transformers, were read for comparison and kept out of the subset counts. Results. Of the 39 subset PRs, 13 merged, 18 were still open, and 8 closed unmerged. Among the 21 resolved PRs, 61.9% merged. Open PRs made up 46% of the subset, the highest share in any part of my record. The merged work clustered around one defect class: silent failure. Code accepted values it should have rejected, dropped errors in background threads, or hid missing data behind a normal response. The hardest case was a long-lived branch. pymilvus #3621 sat open from 20 June 2026 with 12 comments, merge conflicts, and a Developer Certificate of Origin (DCO) gap on a sync commit. Conclusions. The code in this subset was rarely the slow part. Review time was. The fixes that landed shared one pattern: they made a system fail loudly, with an accurate message, at the point where bad data entered. A retrieval system that says "no record found" when it means "the index is corrupt" will mislead a clinician the way a silent defect misleads a developer.

papers.title: CoWalk: Cooperative Walks for Agentic Batch Queries on Disk-Resident Graphs
papers.abstract: Workloads such as query rewriting, deep research and group-relative policy optimization (GRPO) issue batches of semantically related vector queries. Existing disk-resident approximate nearest neighbor (ANN) systems process these queries independently. On three workloads, 31 to 67 percent of the I/Os of a batch fetch a page that another query of the batch has already fetched. A page cache shared by the batch removes these I/Os, yet it makes a single-thread search only $1.1$ to $1.2{\times}$ faster, because the search time goes to distance computation and the cache does not change the walk of any query. We present CoWalk, which runs the queries of a batch as cooperating walks on one thread. Every query keeps its own candidate list, a page is read once per batch, and the full-precision vector on every fetched page is ranked by every query of the batch. A query therefore reaches the target recall with a shorter candidate list, which computes fewer distances and issues fewer I/Os. At recall@10 of 0.95, CoWalk answers a batch on one thread $1.6$ to $1.9{\times}$ faster than the fastest per-query baseline and issues $2.8$ to $6.9{\times}$ fewer I/Os. On a server it serves $3.0$ to $6.9{\times}$ the throughput of that baseline at a similar batch latency.

papers.title: Family Four: Self-verifying vector and GPU retrieval substrate: Same data, same result, verifiable at every step: every index proves it was built from the database it serves.
papers.abstract: Same data, same result, verifiable at every step: every index proves it was built from the database it serves.. Methods and Systems for a Self-Verifying Deterministic Vector Index and GPU Retrieval Substrate Materialized From a Relational System of Record. U.S. Provisional Patent Application No. 64/148,001 (patent pending). Embodied in the vector store of the Inference Fabric. Traditional vector pipelines create multiple copies of data, a source database, a vector store, index files, GPU memory, with no provable link between them. Data can drift, go stale or be corrupted, and nobody can prove what produced a result. Here the relational database is the only authority. Vectors are exported deterministically into memory-mapped shards that serve reads and carry references back to the database; they are serving representations, never another authoritative copy. papers.title: Adaptive Digital Consciousness: An Evolutionary Framework for Human Identity Preservation Using Large Language Models
papers.abstract: Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) and Large Language Models (LLMs) have greatly changed the interaction between man and machines through natural-language reasoning, content generation, personalization, and interaction via agents. However, traditional LLM applications do not provide a unified mechanism for maintaining a long-term, structured, and identity-consistent representation of a person during long-time interaction. As shown in the recent studies of generative agents, long-term LLM memory, agentic memory, lifelong learning, and AI self-identity, these processes present essential capabilities that have been studied as separate components. This paper presents the Adaptive Digital Consciousness (ADC) framework as the theoretical architecture for computational representation of core features of human identity. The ADC framework proposes a system of structured representation of Digital DNA for personal knowledge, experience, preferences, values, and behaviors and connects it to multilayer memory, semantic embeddings, vector retrieval, Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG), LLM reasoning, adaptive learning, and autonomous agents. The framework also proposes the notion of identity constraints and the system of updating memory, consolidating it, handling conflicts, forgetting, maintaining privacy, consent, and security, as well as monitoring the origin of digital information. The goal of the study is not to replicate biological or subjective consciousness The research motivation, previous works, the system suggested, as well as memory and adaptation techniques, evaluation techniques, ethics and applications of the findings, drawbacks of the research and future research directions on this subject.

papers.title: Beyond Similarity Search: Knowledge Graph Metadata Enrichment for Enterprise Retrieval-Augmented Generation
papers.abstract: A key challenge of RAG systems is retrieving information from enterprise documents created by multiple teams over time, where it is not possible to enrich the information using the latest information and metadata available outside the scope of organizational documentation responsibility. We investigated whether using a knowledge graph to store metadata and frequently changing information would improve upon knowledge retrieval over similarity search over embeddings. To perform the experiment, we created a snapshot of the SEC EDGAR dataset for a quarter, comprising 167,050 filings from 10,511 companies and 508,714 embedded chunks of risk-factor text. To simulate the enrichment, we created a knowledge graph of 430,257 nodes and 561,144 edges carrying an accession number on every edge. To evaluate the gain obtained via a graph-based design, we evaluated three architectures: text-to-SQL over typed columns, dense-vector RAG with HNSW cosine search, and a two-stage GraphRAG design. All architectures share the same model and temperature to allow comparison. Results are scored programmatically by an LLM as judge over 20 questions divided across four categories, each question asked three times. GraphRAG solved 16 of 20 questions on all three attempts, compared to 10 for text-to-SQL and 3 for vector RAG. GraphRAG lost on structured aggregation queries. Vector RAG lost the single-document category it was expected to win, passing 3 of 15 where GraphRAG passed 15 of 15, because company attribution is not recoverable from cosine similarity at this scale. All six confident falsehoods in the benchmark were text-to-SQL conflating distinct people who share a surname, the failure that resolving identity to an identifier before reading any text prevents structurally; GraphRAG made none. We claim no advantage beyond this corpus, this model and this question set.

papers.title: ExtenGen: A Lightweight Shared Memory Layer for AI Coding Agents
papers.abstract: Modern software teams increasingly rely on AI coding agents such as Claude Code, Cursor, and Codex to write, review, and debug source code. However, each agent session begins without knowledge of earlier sessions, so that decisions, architectural context, and institutional knowledge distributed across GitHub issues, pull requests, and chat threads are not carried forward. Developers consequently re-explain the same background repeatedly, which consumes time and tokens and produces inconsistent answers across team members. This report presents ExtenGen, a lightweight, self-hostable shared memory layer for AI coding agents. ExtenGen is implemented as a Model Context Protocol (MCP) server that exposes two tools, store_observation and recall_context, and it follows a five-stage pipeline of Capture, Embed, Store, Retrieve, and Inject. Captured text is converted into vector embeddings using the OpenAI text-embedding-3-small model and stored in PostgreSQL with the pgvector extension, while row-level security policies restrict every row to authorised organisations and users. At query time, a cosine-similarity search combined with an access-control filter returns the top-k most relevant authorised observations, which are merged into the agent's prompt. The lightweight version supports two ingestion sources, live MCP agent sessions and GitHub commit and pull requests, and is intended for small-team, self-hosted deployment. The project demonstrates Retrieval-Augmented Generation, vector similarity search, and multi-tenant access control in a single applied system and aims to reduce repeated context explanation and token usage.

papers.title: Spiking Neural Networks Are Harder to Steal: A Benchmark Study of Model Stealing Attacks
papers.abstract: Machine learning models deployed behind query interfaces expose more than their predictions, because an adversary can use those predictions to rebuild the model itself. Model stealing attacks (MSAs) exploit this exposure by training a surrogate model that replicates the decision behavior of a target through black-box queries alone, without access to its parameters or training data. These attacks are well characterized for conventional artificial neural networks (ANNs), yet spiking neural networks (SNNs) process information in a fundamentally different way. SNNs communicate through sparse, discrete spikes, and their outputs depend on membrane potentials that evolve over time rather than on a static mapping from input to output. This temporal mode of computation suggests that the decision behavior of an SNN may be harder to reconstruct from its responses. This work tests that possibility by benchmarking four representative MSAs, namely the Papernot, Tramèr, T-RND, and color perturbation attacks, against SNNs and their ANN counterparts on MNIST, Fashion-MNIST, and CIFAR-10. Across every attack and dataset, SNNs prove consistently more difficult to steal. Surrogates of SNNs achieve 10% to 20% lower agreement with the target model and 15% to 25% lower adversarial transferability than surrogates of ANNs. We attribute this resistance to the way SNNs compute, as their spike-based and time-dependent dynamics yield decision boundaries that ANN-based surrogates struggle to approximate, even under large query budgets. These findings extend the known resilience of SNNs beyond attacks on training data to the replication of model functionality, strengthening the case for neuromorphic architectures in security-sensitive applications.

papers.title: Cumulative Memory Sizing and Asymmetric Latency Dynamics in Local Retrieval-Augmented Generation Pipelines (2026)
papers.abstract: This systems engineering paper models end-to-end memory allocation and pipeline execution latency in air-gapped, on-premises Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) architectures. A persistent operational bottleneck in local AI deployment is isolating generator LLM capacity while neglecting the cumulative VRAM demands of concurrent neural pipeline components. Key research investigations include: Quantitative memory footprint modeling across dense multi-lingual embedding models (BAAI/bge-m3, Nomic Embed v1.5) and high-precision cross-encoder rerankers (bge-reranker-large) co-existing in GPU VRAM. Dynamic Key-Value (KV) cache memory scaling under retrieved-context injection across 4,000 to 32,000 token prompt buffers on 8B, 14B, 32B, and 70B open-weight architectures. Host system RAM consumption and cache behavior of in-memory Hierarchical Navigable Small World (HNSW) vector indexing (Qdrant, ChromaDB) operating with zero GPU VRAM consumption. Hardware sizing bounds establishing minimum viable GPU silicon thresholds (Single RTX 4090 24GB vs. Dual RTX 3090 48GB vs. Apple Silicon Unified Memory). For the complete architectural decision matrix, automated benchmark scripts, and production Python deployment blueprints, access the full publication at TechGuidePro:https://www.besttechguidepro.com/2026/10/local-rag-hardware-vram-sizing-guide.html

papers.title: Embeddings: The Map Without a Cartographer
papers.abstract: The essay starts from Antisthenes, the Socratic who rejected definitions and held that to know what a thing is one must place it among others, and follows that intuition up to embeddings: vectors that place linguistic units in a mathematical space learned from their uses. It explains the embedding matrix, the distributional analysis of Harris and Firth, word2vec and cosine similarity, the analogy king minus man plus woman landing near queen, the Leibnizian dream of a characteristica universalis, latent semantic analysis, GloVe, ELMo and BERT, the attention that redraws the map sentence by sentence, Sentence-BERT and CLIP, vector search and RAG systems. It closes with the strangest part: nobody drew this map or decided in advance what each axis means, the geometry appeared as a result of training, and a map excellent for navigating language may not tell us where the borders that matter in the world are.
